title: Ten Virgins, the Talents, and the Sheep and Goats
summary: Jesus completes his teaching on the Mount of Olives with three pictures of readiness for his return. Ten young women wait for a delayed bridegroom, and only those who brought oil enough go in to the feast; three servants are entrusted with their master's money, and the one who buried his is condemned; and the Son of Man, enthroned as king, separates all the nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, judging them by how they treated the least of his brothers.
story:
Chapter 24 ended with the call to keep watch because no one knows the day or hour, and with a parable of a faithful and a wicked servant whose master is delayed (24:45-51). Chapter 25 continues the same speech without a break. It is the last part of the fifth and final discourse in Matthew, which began when the disciples asked Jesus, as he sat on the Mount of Olives, what would be the sign of his coming and of the end of the age (24:3). The first two parables develop two sides of readiness: being prepared for a long delay, and working faithfully with what has been entrusted. The chapter closes with a scene of final judgment that is the last public teaching of Jesus in Matthew.

The placement matters. In the very next verse Matthew signals that Jesus has finished all these sayings (26:1), and the passion begins. The king who will one day sit on his glorious throne and judge all the nations is about to be judged by a high priest and a Roman governor, to go hungry and thirsty, to be stripped, bound, and held as a prisoner. The chapter's promise of a coming kingdom and its warning of a shut door stand at the threshold of the cross.
historical:
The speech is set a few days before Passover in the spring of about AD 30 or 33, on the Mount of Olives, the ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley from the temple (24:3). Its historical setting is less a single event than the situation Jesus foresees for his followers: an interval between his departure and his return, long enough that some would grow careless and others give up. Three times in two chapters the delay is named: the wicked servant says his master is delayed (24:48), the bridegroom is delayed (25:5), and the master returns after a long time (25:19). Matthew's first readers, writing and reading decades later (the Gospel is usually dated between the 60s and the 90s), knew that interval firsthand, and the parables speak directly to a church that had to learn to wait without losing heart. Second Peter 3:4-9 shows that the delay was already a question in the first century.

The talent was not a coin but a weight, used for silver or gold. The standard varied by region and period, from about 26 kilograms for the Attic talent to somewhat more for others. As money it was reckoned at six thousand drachmas or denarii, and since a denarius was a laborer's pay for a day (20:2), one talent was roughly twenty years of wages, five talents about a century. Josephus gives a sense of scale: after Herod the Great died in 4 BC, Augustus divided his kingdom, and Josephus reports that Archelaus received revenue of six hundred talents a year (the parallel account in Jewish War book 2 gives four hundred), Herod Antipas two hundred, and Philip one hundred (Antiquities 17.318-320). Even the servant with one talent held a fortune, and the servant in 18:24 who owed ten thousand talents owed a sum beyond any private person's reach. Luke tells a related parable with minas, each worth a hundred denarii (Luke 19:11-27); the two share the pattern of a departing master, entrusted money, a reckoning, and a condemned servant, but differ in amounts, number of servants, and setting.

The master's words about the bankers (trapezitai, literally ‘table men’, the same people who changed money at tables in the temple courts, 21:12) reflect ordinary finance in the Roman world, where money could be deposited with bankers who paid interest. The Law of Moses forbade Israelites to charge interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:35-37, Deuteronomy 23:19-20), but the parable is told from the viewpoint of a master who expects a return, and it neither commends nor condemns the practice. Burying money was a recognized way of keeping it safe in a world without secure vaults; Matthew himself tells of treasure hidden in a field (13:44). The Babylonian Talmud later records the ruling of the sage Samuel that money entrusted to someone can be properly guarded only by burying it in the ground (b. Bava Metzia 42a). By that standard the third servant took the legally safest course, which makes the master's verdict all the sharper: caution was not the virtue he wanted.

The judgment scene draws on a picture known from Jewish writing of the period. Daniel 7:13-14 shows one like a son of man receiving everlasting dominion from the Ancient of Days. The Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37-71), a Jewish work whose date is debated (most scholars place it around the turn of the eras) and which is absent from the Dead Sea Scrolls, repeatedly describe the Son of Man or Chosen One sitting on the throne of his glory to judge kings and the mighty (1 Enoch 62:2-5, 69:27-29). Matthew uses the same phrase, the throne of his glory, at 19:28 and 25:31.
cultural:
Village weddings followed a familiar pattern. After the betrothal, which was already a binding marriage (1:18-19), the bridegroom went to the bride's family home, and after celebration he brought her in procession to his own house, often at night, where the feast took place. First Maccabees 9:37-39 describes a wedding party escorting a bride with drums and music, and the bridegroom coming out with his friends and brothers to meet them. The ten young women (parthenoi, unmarried girls, usually translated virgins or bridesmaids) are friends of the family who wait to join the procession with lights and escort the couple in. Their lamps (lampades) may have been small clay oil lamps, which burn for hours on a filling, or torches made of rags soaked in oil on a pole, which needed frequent re-soaking; Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus) argued for torches, and interpreters remain divided. Either way the oil ran low during a long wait, and anyone without a flask of reserve (angeion, verse 4) would miss the procession. Once the door of the house was shut the feast was closed, as in Luke 13:25, and the bridegroom's reply, I do not know you, is a formula of refusal that echoes 7:23. The foolish women are sent to buy oil at midnight, and the comedy of that errand is part of the point: some preparation cannot be made at the last minute or borrowed from someone else.

The judgment scene assumes a shepherd's world. In the land of Israel sheep and goats often grazed together in mixed flocks and were separated when needed, for milking, shearing, or shelter, a sight every hearer had seen. The right hand was the place of honor and favor (1 Kings 2:19, Psalm 110:1), the left the place of lesser standing. Ezekiel had already pictured God as a shepherd who judges between one sheep and another, between rams and goats (Ezekiel 34:17).

The six works of mercy belong to Israel's long tradition of piety. Isaiah 58:7 names sharing bread with the hungry, bringing the homeless poor into one's house, and clothing the naked as the fast God chooses; Job defends his life by the same deeds (Job 31:16-20, 31:32), and Ezekiel counts them marks of the righteous man (Ezekiel 18:7). Tobit remembers giving bread to the hungry, clothing the naked, and burying the dead (Tobit 1:16-17), and Sirach urges visiting the sick (Sirach 7:35). The Talmud teaches that to walk after God is to imitate his deeds: to clothe the naked as he clothed Adam, to visit the sick as he visited Abraham, to comfort mourners, and to bury the dead (b. Sotah 14a). A midrash on Psalm 118:19-20 imagines that in the world to come a person is asked what his work was, and when he answers that he fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, or clothed the naked, the gate of the Lord is opened to him (Midrash Tehillim 118.17). Even the Egyptian Book of the Dead, in the declarations of spell 125, has the deceased claim to have given bread to the hungry, water to the thirsty, and clothing to the naked. What is new in Matthew is not the list but the identity of the one who receives the deeds: the king himself.

Prison in the ancient world was usually a place of holding before trial or punishment, not a sentence in itself, and prisoners depended on family and friends for food and clothing. Visiting them was a lifeline, and it could be dangerous to be seen with them. Paul thanks Onesiphorus for searching him out in Rome and not being ashamed of his chains (2 Timothy 1:16-17), and Hebrews urges readers to remember prisoners as if chained with them (Hebrews 13:3). The pagan satirist Lucian, around 165, mocks Christians for crowding to the prison with meals and gifts when the charlatan Peregrinus was jailed (The Passing of Peregrinus 12-13), unwitting testimony that this chapter shaped how early Christians behaved.
literary:
Chapter 25 completes the second half of the discourse that began at 24:4. After the warnings about the temple's fall and the coming of the Son of Man (24:4-35), Jesus turns to how disciples should live in the meantime (24:36-25:46) through a sequence of short parables: the days of Noah (24:37-41), the thief in the night (24:43-44), the faithful and wicked servant (24:45-51), the ten virgins (25:1-13), and the talents (25:14-30), crowned by the judgment of the nations (25:31-46). The ten virgins and the judgment scene are found only in Matthew; the talents has a partner in Luke's minas. The whole unit closes with the formula that ends each of Matthew's five discourses (26:1).

The two parables are built alike. Each divides its characters into the ready and the unready (five wise and five foolish; two faithful servants and one wicked), each turns on an arrival after a delay, and each ends in exclusion: a shut door, outer darkness. Both use the contrast of wise and foolish that closed the Sermon on the Mount (7:24-27), and the word for wise, phronimos, links the virgins to the wise and faithful servant of 24:45. In the talents, the first two servants' reports and the master's replies are repeated almost word for word (verses 20-23), so that the third servant's different speech stands out, and the parable closes with a proverb Jesus used earlier of understanding the kingdom (verse 29, compare 13:12).

The judgment scene is not strictly a parable, though it contains a simile (the shepherd), and it moves from the Son of Man (verse 31) to the King (verse 34), the only place in the Gospels where Jesus calls himself king in his own teaching. It is built on repetition: the list of six needs is spoken four times, by the king to each group and by each group in reply, each time a little shorter, until in verse 44 the condemned run them together in a single breath. The repetition slows the reader and makes the surprise of both groups the heart of the scene: neither the righteous nor the condemned knew that they had been dealing with the king. There is also an asymmetry the reader should notice. The kingdom was prepared for the blessed from the foundation of the world (verse 34), but the fire was prepared for the devil and his angels (verse 41), not for human beings.

outline.t: The parable of the ten virgins
The Son of Man judges the nations

doctrines.note: All three scenes assume that the Son of Man will come again, at an hour no one knows, after a delay long enough to test his people (verses 5, 13, 19, 31). Readiness is not calculating the date but keeping oil in store, working with what has been entrusted, and showing mercy, so that the coming finds disciples awake.

Every nation will be gathered before the Son of Man, and he will separate people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats (verses 31-33). The judgment is personal, public, and final, and its standard is how people treated the king in the persons of the least of his brothers.

The hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick, and the prisoner stand at the center of the last judgment, and the king counts what was done or not done to them as done or not done to himself (verses 40 and 45). Whatever one concludes about who the least are, the chapter makes neglect of the needy a matter of eternal weight.

The foolish virgins are shut out, the worthless servant is thrown into the outer darkness, and those on the left go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (verses 12, 30, 41, 46). Christians differ on the nature and duration of final punishment, but the chapter leaves no doubt that exclusion from the kingdom is real and that the fire was not prepared for human beings.

The kingdom is pictured as a wedding feast, as the joy of the master, and as an inheritance prepared from the foundation of the world (verses 10, 21, 34). God's purpose for his people was settled before history began, and the end of the story is a feast, a welcome, and a kingdom.

words.note: Numphios, bridegroom. It occurs sixteen times in the New Testament, four of them in this parable (verses 1, 5, 6, 10). Jesus used it of himself when asked why his disciples did not fast (9:15), drawing on the prophets' picture of God as Israel's husband (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:19-20), and John the Baptist uses it of Jesus in John 3:29. In the parable the long-awaited bridegroom stands for the Son of Man at his coming, and the feast for the kingdom.

Phronimos, wise, sensible, shrewd. It occurs fourteen times in the New Testament, seven of them in Matthew. BDAG describes it as practical wisdom, the good sense that sees what a situation requires, rather than learning. In Matthew it marks the man who builds on rock (7:24), the disciples sent out shrewd as serpents (10:16), the faithful servant (24:45), and the five virgins who brought oil (25:2, 4, 8, 9). Its opposite here, mōros, foolish, is the word of 7:26.

Grēgoreō, to stay awake, keep watch. It occurs twenty-two times in the New Testament and six times in Matthew, all in chapters 24 to 26. The command that ends the virgins' parable (verse 13) repeats 24:42, and in Gethsemane Jesus will ask Peter, James, and John to keep watch with him and find them sleeping (26:38-41). In the parable all ten fall asleep; what distinguishes the wise is not that they never slept but that they were ready when the cry came.

Talanton, talent, a weight of silver or gold used as a unit of money, worth about six thousand denarii. It occurs fourteen times in the New Testament, all in Matthew (18:24 and thirteen times in this parable). The English word talent, meaning a natural ability, comes from medieval readings of this parable. In the story itself it is money, standing for whatever the master entrusts, which interpreters have taken to include gifts and abilities but also the gospel, the knowledge of God's will, and opportunities to serve.

Elachistos, least, smallest, the superlative of mikros, little. It occurs fourteen times in the New Testament and five times in Matthew: Bethlehem is by no means least (2:6); whoever relaxes the least commandment will be called least in the kingdom (5:19); and here, the least of these brothers of mine (verses 40 and 45). It is closely related to the little ones (mikroi) who belong to Jesus, whom Matthew names in 10:42 and 18:6-14, which bears directly on the debate about who the least are.

Adelphos, brother, used more than 340 times in the New Testament, of blood brothers, of fellow Israelites, and of fellow members of God's family. In Matthew Jesus calls those who do his Father's will his brother and sister and mother (12:49-50), tells his disciples that they are all brothers (23:8), and after the resurrection calls them my brothers (28:10). Those who read the least as disciples point to this usage; those who read them as any needy person note that the king speaks as the one who identifies with the lowly, and that brothers in the Greek plural can include sisters.

Aiōnios, eternal, literally belonging to the age, meaning the age to come. It occurs about seventy times in the New Testament. In verse 46 the same adjective describes both the punishment and the life, and in verse 41 the fire. Lexicons agree that it describes what belongs to the coming age; they differ in how much it says in itself about unending duration, which is why the word is central to the debate over final punishment. Augustine (City of God 21.23) argued that the parallel in verse 46 requires the two to last equally long.

Kolasis, punishment. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, here and in 1 John 4:18 (fear has to do with punishment). In older Greek it could mean pruning or correction, and some universalist readers have stressed that sense; others reply that by the first century it was commonly used of penalty in general, without any sense of improvement. The context of verse 46, set against eternal life, gives it the weight of final judgment.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus in three roles that belong to God in the Old Testament. He is the bridegroom whose coming opens the wedding feast, the role the prophets gave to the LORD in his love for Israel (Isaiah 54:5, 62:5; Hosea 2:19-20). He is the master who entrusts his wealth to his servants and returns to settle accounts. And above all he is the Son of Man seated on his glorious throne, attended by all the angels, gathering all the nations before him, the King who judges. This last picture draws on Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom from the Ancient of Days, and on Ezekiel 34, where God himself shepherds his flock, judges between sheep and goats, and sets over them one shepherd, his servant David (Ezekiel 34:17, 34:23-24). Jesus claims both roles at once: the divine shepherd and the Davidic king. He speaks of God as My Father (verse 34) and places his own welcome or refusal at the door of eternity.

Yet the King identifies himself with the hungry, the stranger, and the prisoner. The words I was hungry, I was a stranger, I was in prison are spoken by the judge of all the earth. The identification is deeper than sympathy. When the risen Christ confronts Saul on the Damascus road, he asks why Saul is persecuting him, not his followers (Acts 9:4-5), and Paul will call the church Christ's body (1 Corinthians 12:27). And within days of this speech the King will go the way of the least himself. He will be seized at night, bound and handed over (27:2), stripped of his clothes (27:28, 27:35), given sour wine when he is thirsty (27:48), and crucified outside the city like a stranger. The one who will judge the nations is judged by them first, and his death is the means by which the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world is opened to those who were never worthy of it.

The two parables also point to him. The bridegroom's delay and sudden arrival keep the church looking for Jesus himself, not for a date, and the master's joy (verses 21 and 23) is the joy the church confesses Christ has with his Father and shares with his people (John 15:11, Hebrews 12:2). The church's confession that he will come again to judge the living and the dead, which the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds make an article of faith, rests heavily on this chapter.
interpretation:
The chapter was read from the beginning as a call to watchfulness and mercy. The Didache, a church manual from around AD 100, closes with a warning to watch over one's life and not let one's lamps go out (Didache 16.1). Origen, in his commentary on Matthew, read the ten virgins allegorically, the five wise and five foolish as the senses rightly or wrongly used. John Chrysostom, preaching at Antioch around 390 (Homilies on Matthew 78 and 79), took the oil to be almsgiving and warned that virginity without mercy could not open the door, and he pressed the sheep and goats on his hearers as a summons to feed Christ in the poor. Augustine (Sermon 93) read the oil as love kept alive within, the inward joy of a good conscience, and in the City of God (21.23) he used verse 46 to argue that punishment is as lasting as life. Sulpicius Severus, in his Life of Martin (chapter 3), tells how the young soldier Martin cut his cloak in half for a freezing beggar at the gate of Amiens and that night saw Christ wearing it, a story that made verse 40 one of the most retold verses of the Middle Ages. The Rule of Benedict (chapters 36 and 53) bids monks care for the sick and receive every guest as Christ, citing this chapter.

Medieval Christianity turned the scene into a system and into stone. The six deeds of verses 35 and 36, with burying the dead added from Tobit, became the seven corporal works of mercy, taught in catechisms and painted by Caravaggio in The Seven Works of Mercy (about 1607, Pio Monte della Misericordia, Naples). The wise and foolish virgins stand in rows on Gothic cathedral portals such as Magdeburg (about 1250) and Strasbourg (late thirteenth century), and the eleventh-century Latin and Occitan drama Sponsus, from the region of Limoges, stages the parable. Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel (1536 to 1541) is the most famous of countless doom paintings shaped by verses 31 to 46.

The Reformers read the chapter within their debate over grace and works. Luther and Calvin insisted that the works of mercy reveal a faith already given rather than earn the kingdom, noting that the kingdom is an inheritance prepared in advance, and Calvin read the talents as all the gifts God gives for the service of others. The English word talent, meaning ability, grew from this reading, and John Milton's sonnet on his blindness (written in the 1650s) turns on the one talent it would be death to hide. Philipp Nicolai's hymn Wachet auf (1599), sung on the virgins' Sunday, became the basis of J. S. Bach's cantata BWV 140, first performed in Leipzig on 25 November 1731.

Modern scholarship has argued most about the least of these. Sherman W. Gray's history of interpretation, The Least of My Brothers (1989), found that before the modern period most interpreters took the least to be Christians, often poor Christians, while a fully universal reading became common only in the twentieth century. Graham Stanton (A Gospel for a New People, 1992), R. T. France, and W. D. Davies and Dale Allison defend the reading that the least are Jesus' disciples; Catholic social teaching, much modern preaching, and liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez (A Theology of Liberation, 1971) read the passage as Christ's identification with all the poor. The talents have also been reread. William R. Herzog II (Parables as Subversive Speech, 1994) argued that Jesus' peasant hearers would have heard the master as a rapacious landlord and the third servant as a whistle-blower, a reading most commentators judge contrary to Matthew's framing but which has pressed readers to notice how the parable sounds to the poor. Jewish scholars in The Jewish Annotated New Testament (2011) point to the rabbinic parallels in the Midrash on Psalms and in the parable of Yohanan ben Zakkai about a king who invited his servants to a banquet without naming the hour, where the wise dressed and waited at the door and the foolish went about their work (b. Shabbat 153a).

In worship the three sections close the church year. The Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman lectionary read the virgins and the talents on the last Sundays after Pentecost in Year A and the sheep and goats on the feast of Christ the King, which Pius XI instituted in 1925.
text:
English Bibles differ in this chapter more by translation than by manuscripts, but a few manuscript differences show through. In verse 1 Codex Bezae, Codex Koridethi (Θ), and many Latin and Syriac copies read that the virgins went out to meet ‘the bridegroom and the bride’. Most early Greek manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lack the addition, and editors judge it a scribal attempt to make the scene match a procession from the bride's house. In verse 13 later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add ‘wherein the Son of man cometh’, drawn from 24:44; the earliest omit it. In verse 31 the King James Version's ‘all the holy angels’ follows later manuscripts, where the earliest have simply ‘all the angels’. In verse 41 Codex Bezae and several Latin witnesses read ‘which my Father prepared’ instead of the simple passive ‘prepared’, a reading that makes the asymmetry with verse 34 disappear.

Translation choices are more visible. The parthenoi of verse 1 are ‘virgins’ in the King James, ESV, and BSB, ‘bridesmaids’ in the NIV, NRSV, and NLT; the Greek word means young unmarried women, and the story is about their role in a wedding, not their sexual status. The NIV (2011) renders the talent as ‘bags of gold’, trying to convey its size, where most versions keep ‘talent’. In verse 40 the King James and ESV have ‘the least of these my brethren’ or ‘brothers’, the NIV ‘the least of these brothers and sisters of mine’, and the NRSV ‘the least of these who are members of my family’. All render the same plural adelphoi, which in Greek can include women; the choice affects how easily a reader hears the reference to Jesus' family of disciples. In verse 46 older and some modern versions have ‘everlasting punishment’, others ‘eternal punishment’, for the same adjective aiōnios.

teach.big: Because the Son of Man will surely come, though later than expected, his people are to be ready, faithful with what he has entrusted, and merciful to the least, for at the end he will count what was done for them as done for him.

outline.t: All ten waited and all ten slept; the difference between wise and foolish lay in preparation for a long delay.
Some readiness cannot be borrowed at the last minute; each person must answer for their own lamp.
The door that opens to a feast also shuts, so keep watch, since no one knows the day or hour.
The master entrusts great wealth according to each servant's ability, and faithfulness means putting it to work at once.
Faithfulness in a few things is met with greater trust and an invitation into the master's joy, whatever the size of the original gift.
The third servant's failure grew from a false picture of his master, and fear that buries what God has given is judged as unfaithfulness.
The Son of Man will sit as King and Shepherd over all the nations, and the final separation belongs to him alone.
The blessed inherit a kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world, and they are surprised to learn that their mercy to the least was mercy to Christ.
Neglect of the least is neglect of Christ, and the outcome of the judgment is eternal in both directions.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first allegorizes every detail of the virgins' parable: the oil as the Holy Spirit, the sellers as priests, the ten as a symbol of completeness. Parables usually make one or two main points, and here the point is stated in verse 13. Neither should the refusal of the wise to share be preached as a lesson in selfishness or in prudence about lending; it makes the point that readiness cannot be transferred.

The talents are often reduced to a sermon on natural abilities, or read as an endorsement of investment, capitalism, or prosperity. The parable assumes an economy of its day but its subject is faithfulness to an absent master, and in context the entrusted goods include the gospel and the whole life of discipleship. Teachers should also resist turning the third servant's description of his master into a statement about God's character. The master does not accept the description; he judges the servant by his own words, and the servant's fear is his undoing.

The judgment scene is misused in opposite directions. Some preach it as salvation by social action, as if eternal life were earned by charity; others explain it away as a warning only to unbelievers or only about treatment of missionaries, so that it makes no claim on Christians' care for the poor. The debate about who the least are is real and should be presented fairly, but on either reading the king holds his people to account for mercy. Finally, avoid both sensationalizing and silencing verse 46. Christians disagree about the nature of final punishment, but the chapter's warning is plain, and it is spoken by the one who also holds out an inheritance prepared from the foundation of the world.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on the anxious and the scrupulous, who may hear the shut door and the outer darkness as aimed at them and wonder whether they have enough oil. Teach that the virgins' parable is a call to readiness, not a riddle designed to keep believers in doubt, and that the servants who were welcomed had simply been faithful with what they had. People who feel they have few gifts, or who live with disability or chronic illness, may hear the talents as a rebuke; the parable gives each servant according to his ability and praises the two-talent servant in exactly the same words as the five-talent servant. The judgment scene may reach people in the room who are hungry, homeless, sick, or in prison, or who love someone who is; teach it so that they hear the King's identification with them, not only a lesson about others. Those who fear hell, or who grieve people who died without faith, need honesty rather than evasion, and the reminder that the judge is the one who died for the least.

hard.q: Who are the least of these brothers of mine, and does this passage teach that people are saved by good deeds?
hard.a:
The strongest objection comes from two directions. Some Christian readers, and many readers outside the church, take the passage at face value: the nations are judged by works of mercy alone, with no mention of faith, grace, or Christ, so the scene seems to teach that anyone who helps the poor is saved and anyone who does not is lost, whatever they believe. Jewish readers have pointed out that this sounds very like the rabbinic teaching that deeds of loving-kindness open the gates of the world to come (Midrash Tehillim 118.17), and some ask why Christians who stress faith alone have so often read the passage as if it said something else. On the other side, some scholars argue that the universal reading of the least, as all the poor, is a modern development that Matthew never intended: Sherman Gray's survey (1989) found it rare before the twentieth century.

On who the least are, there are two main readings. The first, defended by Graham Stanton, R. T. France, D. A. Carson, and W. D. Davies and Dale Allison, holds that the least are Jesus' disciples. In Matthew Jesus calls those who do his Father's will his brothers (12:49-50, 28:10), promises that whoever gives a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is a disciple will not lose his reward (10:42), and says that whoever receives his messengers receives him (10:40). On this reading the nations are judged by how they received Christ's needy, often persecuted, messengers, a message of comfort to a church facing hostility. The second reading, held across much of modern Catholic, Protestant, and Orthodox teaching and by liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez, holds that the least are any people in need. It points out that the list of needs is universal, that the scene judges all the nations, that the righteous are surprised (which is odd if they knowingly helped Christians), and that Jesus elsewhere commands love of enemies and neighbors without limit (5:44, Luke 10:25-37). Both readings have strong defenders, and both make care for the vulnerable a mark of belonging to the king.

On salvation, most interpreters in every tradition deny that the passage teaches that eternal life is earned. The righteous inherit a kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world (verse 34), an inheritance and not wages, and they are surprised by the verdict. Augustine, Luther, and Calvin read the deeds as evidence of a life already turned toward Christ, as a tree is known by its fruit (7:16-20, 12:33). Catholic theology, following the Council of Trent (1547), speaks of good works done in grace as truly meritorious while insisting that grace is their source. The passage belongs with Jesus' other warnings that calling him Lord is not enough (7:21-23), and with James 2:14-17. The church's confession that salvation is by grace stands beside this passage's warning that faith which never feeds the hungry or visits the prisoner is not the faith Jesus recognizes. How these fit together in detail is one of the places where Protestant and Catholic readers still differ.

hard.q: Does verse 46 teach that punishment lasts forever, and how can eternal punishment be just?
hard.a:
The objection is moral and exegetical at once. Morally, critics from the Enlightenment onward, and many Christians, have asked how finite sins in a short life could deserve endless suffering, and how a God of love could sustain it. Bertrand Russell, in Why I Am Not a Christian (1927), counted Christ's teaching on hell a defect in his moral character. Exegetically, some argue that the adjective aiōnios means belonging to the age to come rather than endless in itself, and that kolasis could mean corrective punishment. David Bentley Hart (That All Shall Be Saved, 2019) argues on these grounds for universal salvation, standing in a line that runs back to Origen and Gregory of Nyssa. Edward Fudge (The Fire That Consumes, 1982), John Stott in Evangelical Essentials (1988), and others argue for conditional immortality: the punishment is eternal in its result, the final destruction of the wicked, not in unending conscious experience.

The traditional reading, taught by Augustine (City of God 21.23), Thomas Aquinas, the Reformers, and the major Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant confessions, holds that verse 46 sets eternal punishment in exact parallel to eternal life, so that if the one is endless the other must be too. Its defenders argue that sin against an infinitely holy God is not finite in its gravity, that the lost remain in rebellion, and that the image of fire prepared for the devil and his angels (verse 41) is set alongside Revelation 20:10. Defenders of each alternative answer that the parallel concerns the finality of the outcome, not identical modes of existence, and that other biblical images (destruction, perishing, the second death) must be weighed alongside this one. Conditionalism and universalism both have serious scholarly defenders; conditionalism in particular has gained ground among evangelicals, while universalism remains a minority position rejected by most churches, and the anathemas against Origenist teaching associated with the Second Council of Constantinople (553) rejected the restoration of all things.

What all these readers agree on is that the chapter speaks of a real and final judgment, that the kingdom was prepared for human beings and the fire was not, and that Jesus spoke these words not to satisfy curiosity but to warn and to call people to mercy. The church confesses that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead; the nature and duration of final punishment is a question on which faithful Christians still differ, and this note does not settle it.

observe: What did the wise virgins do that the foolish ones did not, and what did all ten of them do while the bridegroom was delayed?
What reason does the third servant give for hiding his talent, and how does the master answer him?
List the six needs the King names. What do both groups ask him, and what does he answer each?
interpret: Why do you think the wise virgins would not share their oil? What does their refusal say about the kind of readiness Jesus has in mind?
The first two servants receive identical praise though they gained different amounts. What does that suggest about how God measures faithfulness?
Who do you think the least of these brothers are, and how does your answer change the way you read the passage?
apply: If the Son of Man came today, what in your life would look like the oil you had failed to bring?
What has God entrusted to you that fear or caution has kept buried?
Where in your city or church are the hungry, the stranger, the sick, and the prisoner, and what would it look like to meet Christ there this month?
